metadata.title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds
metadata.authors: Eugene F. Fama and Kenneth R. French
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.
metadata.registry_mismatch_note: PDF matches expected title (Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds, Fama & French 1993).

nodes.name: Cross-Section of Average Stock and Bond Returns
nodes.statement: Identify a small set of common risk factors $f_1,\ldots,f_K$ such that, for any asset $i$, the time-series regression $R_i(t)-RF(t)=\alpha_i+\sum_k \beta_{ik} f_k(t)+e_i(t)$ has $\alpha_i\approx 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Find a small set of common risk factors whose time-series regressions explain the cross-section of average excess returns on stocks and bonds, with intercepts close to zero.

nodes.name: Excess Return
nodes.statement: For asset $i$ in month $t$, the excess return is $R_i(t)-RF(t)$, where $RF(t)$ is the one-month Treasury bill rate observed at the beginning of month $t$.

nodes.name: Book-to-Market Equity (BE/ME)
nodes.statement: For a firm in fiscal year $t-1$, $BE/ME$ is the book common equity $BE$ (COMPUSTAT stockholders' equity plus balance-sheet deferred taxes and investment tax credit, minus the book value of preferred stock) divided by market equity $ME$ at the end of December of $t-1$. Negative-$BE$ firms are excluded.

nodes.name: Size (ME)
nodes.statement: The size of a stock in June of year $t$ is $ME=$ stock price times number of shares outstanding at the end of June of $t$.

nodes.name: Six Size-BE/ME Building-Block Portfolios
nodes.statement: Each June of $t$, NYSE/Amex/NASDAQ stocks are split by NYSE median $ME$ into Small/Big and by NYSE 30/40/30 $BE/ME$ breakpoints into Low/Medium/High; the six value-weighted portfolios $S/L,S/M,S/H,B/L,B/M,B/H$ are the intersections.

nodes.name: TERM (Term-Structure Factor)
nodes.statement: $TERM(t) = LTG(t) - RF(t-1)$, the difference between the monthly long-term government bond return $LTG$ and the one-month Treasury bill rate $RF$ measured at the end of the previous month.
nodes.statement_clean: Long-term government bond return minus the one-month T-bill rate; proxy for unexpected shifts in interest rates.

nodes.name: DEF (Default Factor)
nodes.statement: $DEF(t) = CB(t) - LTG(t)$, where $CB$ is the return on a market portfolio of long-term corporate bonds (Ibbotson Composite) and $LTG$ is the long-term government bond return.
nodes.statement_clean: Return on long-term corporate bonds minus return on long-term government bonds; proxy for shifts in default risk.

nodes.name: SMB (Small Minus Big)
nodes.statement: $SMB(t) = \tfrac{1}{3}(R_{S/L}+R_{S/M}+R_{S/H}) - \tfrac{1}{3}(R_{B/L}+R_{B/M}+R_{B/H})$, the monthly difference between the average return of the three small-stock and the three big-stock building-block portfolios.
nodes.statement_clean: Mimicking return for the size factor: average of three small-stock portfolios minus average of three big-stock portfolios with similar weighted-average BE/ME.

nodes.name: HML (High Minus Low)
nodes.statement: $HML(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}(R_{S/H}+R_{B/H}) - \tfrac{1}{2}(R_{S/L}+R_{B/L})$, the monthly difference between the average return on the two high-$BE/ME$ portfolios and the two low-$BE/ME$ portfolios.
nodes.statement_clean: Mimicking return for the book-to-market factor: average of two high-BE/ME portfolios minus average of two low-BE/ME portfolios with similar weighted-average size.

nodes.name: Excess Market Return RM-RF
nodes.statement: $RM-RF$, where $RM$ is the value-weighted return on all stocks in the six size-$BE/ME$ portfolios plus the negative-$BE$ stocks excluded from those portfolios, and $RF$ is the one-month Treasury bill rate.

nodes.name: 25 Size-BE/ME Stock Portfolios
nodes.statement: Each June of $t$, NYSE/Amex/NASDAQ stocks are sorted by $ME$ and (independently) by $BE/ME$ into NYSE-breakpoint quintiles; the 25 value-weighted portfolios are the intersections of the five size and five $BE/ME$ groups.

nodes.name: Bond Test Portfolios
nodes.statement: Two government-bond maturity groups (1-5 years and 6-10 years) from CRSP, plus five Moody's rating groups (Aaa, Aa, A, Baa, LG=below Baa) of corporate bonds from Ibbotson; excess returns are dependent variables in the time-series regressions.

nodes.name: RMO (Orthogonalized Market Factor)
nodes.statement: $RMO$ is the sum of the intercept and residuals from regression (1) of $RM-RF$ on $SMB$, $HML$, $TERM$, $DEF$; by construction $RMO$ is uncorrelated with these four explanatory variables.

nodes.name: RM-RF Decomposition Regression
nodes.statement: $RM-RF = 0.50 + 0.44\,SMB - 0.63\,HML + 0.81\,TERM + 0.79\,DEF + e$, with $R^2=0.38$ over 342 monthly observations (July 1963 - December 1991).
nodes.statement_clean: Regression of the excess market return on SMB, HML, TERM, DEF gives strong loadings on all four factors and R-squared of 0.38, showing the market portfolio is a hodgepodge of common factors.

nodes.name: Three-Factor Stock Regression
nodes.statement: $R_i(t)-RF(t) = a_i + b_i\,[RM(t)-RF(t)] + s_i\,SMB(t) + h_i\,HML(t) + e_i(t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Time-series regression of an excess stock return on the three stock-market factors RM-RF, SMB, HML.

nodes.name: Five-Factor Regression
nodes.statement: $R_i(t)-RF(t) = a_i + b_i\,[RM(t)-RF(t)] + s_i\,SMB(t) + h_i\,HML(t) + m_i\,TERM(t) + d_i\,DEF(t) + e_i(t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Time-series regression on the three stock-market factors plus the two bond-market factors.

nodes.name: Bond-Market Two-Factor Regression
nodes.statement: $R_i(t)-RF(t) = a_i + m_i\,TERM(t) + d_i\,DEF(t) + e_i(t)$.

nodes.name: Residual Predictability Test
nodes.statement: $e_i(t+1) = k_0 + k_1\,D(t)/P(t) + k_2\,DFS(t) + k_3\,TS(t) + k_4\,RF(t) + \eta_i(t+1)$, where $e_i$ are residuals from the five-factor regression of table 7.
nodes.statement_clean: Regress five-factor residuals on dividend yield, default spread, term spread, and short rate to test whether known predictors of returns survive in the residuals.

nodes.name: GRS F-Statistic for Joint Intercepts
nodes.statement: $F = (A'\Sigma^{-1}A)\,(N-K-L+1)/(L\,(N-K)\,\omega_{\alpha\alpha})$, with $N=342$ months, $L=32$ regressions, $K=1+$#explanatory variables, $A$ the vector of 32 intercepts, $\Sigma$ the residual covariance, and $\omega_{\alpha\alpha}$ the $(X'X)^{-1}$ element corresponding to the intercept; under normality and zero true intercepts, $F$ is $F$-distributed with $L$ and $N-K-L+1$ d.f.

nodes.name: Multifactor Asset-Pricing Implication (Merton 1973 / Ross 1976)
nodes.statement: If the explanatory returns are good mimicking portfolios for the underlying common risk factors, the multifactor asset-pricing models of Merton and Ross imply that intercepts in the time-series regressions of excess returns on the mimicking portfolio returns are zero (exactly in Merton, approximately in Ross).
assumptions: Explanatory returns have minimal firm-specific variance and mimic the underlying state variables/common risk factors
conclusions: Time-series intercepts $\alpha_i$ in the regression of excess returns on mimicking portfolio returns are indistinguishable from $0$
nodes.origin_citation: Merton 1973 (ICAPM); Ross 1976 (APT); approximation noted by Shanken 1982

nodes.name: Sharpe-Lintner CAPM
nodes.statement: Under the Sharpe-Lintner CAPM, the cross-section of average excess returns is fully explained by market $\beta$, with $E[R_i]-RF = \beta_i\,(E[RM]-RF)$ and the intercept in a one-factor excess-return regression equal to zero.

nodes.name: GRS F-Test of Zero Intercepts
nodes.statement: Under the assumption that returns and explanatory variables are jointly normal and the true intercepts are $0$, the statistic $F$ in EP371.6 has an exact $F$-distribution with $L$ and $N-K-L+1$ degrees of freedom.
assumptions: Returns and explanatory variables are jointly normal
conclusions: $F\sim F_{L,\,N-K-L+1}$, providing an exact joint test of $\alpha_1=\cdots=\alpha_L=0$

nodes.name: Five-Factor Description of Stock and Bond Returns
nodes.statement: Three stock-market factors ($RM-RF$, $SMB$, $HML$) and two bond-market factors ($TERM$, $DEF$) capture the common variation in stock and bond returns; together their average premiums explain the cross-section of average returns on the 25 size-$BE/ME$ stock portfolios and the seven bond portfolios.
assumptions: Sample: monthly returns July 1963 - December 1991, 342 months
32 test assets: 25 size-$BE/ME$ stock portfolios and 7 bond portfolios
conclusions: Stock returns share variation through three stock-market factors
Bond returns are dominated by $TERM$ and $DEF$ (except low-grade corporates which also load on stock factors)
Stock and bond returns are linked through the two term-structure factors

nodes.name: Three-Factor Model Explains Cross-Section of Average Stock Returns
nodes.statement: In the three-factor regression $R_i-RF = a_i + b_i(RM-RF)+s_i\,SMB + h_i\,HML + e_i$, the 25 size-$BE/ME$ portfolios produce intercepts close to $0$ (only 2 of 25 exceed $0.2\%$ per month, 16 within $0.1\%$ of $0$); SMB and HML absorb the size and book-to-market effects in average returns.
conclusions: $RM-RF$, $SMB$, $HML$ jointly capture the cross-section of average stock returns
Market factor explains the average stock-bill spread; $SMB$ and $HML$ explain cross-sectional spread across stocks

nodes.name: TERM and DEF Capture Bond Common Variation
nodes.statement: Used as the only explanatory variables, $TERM$ and $DEF$ produce $R^2$ from $0.49$ (LG) to $0.97$-$0.98$ (high-grade corporates) for the seven bond portfolios; $t$-statistics on $TERM$ slopes for bonds exceed 18 and on $DEF$ slopes exceed 7.8.

nodes.name: TERM and DEF Also Capture Common Variation in Stock Returns
nodes.statement: All 25 stock portfolios produce $TERM$ slopes greater than 5 standard errors above $0$ and $DEF$ slopes greater than 3.5 standard errors above $0$; $TERM$ slopes for stocks (near 1) match those for long-term bonds.

nodes.name: Five-Factor Regressions Reveal Term-Structure Factors in Stocks
nodes.statement: When $RMO$ replaces $RM-RF$, the five-factor regressions for stocks produce $TERM$ slopes more than 14 standard errors from $0$ and $DEF$ slopes more than 7 standard errors from $0$; $TERM$ and $DEF$ slopes for stocks resemble those for bonds, showing the term-structure factors are common to both markets.

nodes.name: Joint F-Test on Three-Factor Model
nodes.statement: The GRS $F$-test on the 32 portfolio intercepts from the three-factor model rejects the zero-intercepts hypothesis at the $0.95$ level (bootstrap $p=0.951$, $F$-distribution $p=0.961$); the rejection is driven mainly by the smallest stocks in the lowest-$BE/ME$ quintile.

nodes.name: Five-Factor Residuals Are Not Predictable
nodes.statement: Estimating regression EP371.5 of five-factor residuals on $D/P$, $DFS$, $TS$, $RF$ produces 15 of 32 negative adjusted-$R^2$ values, only 4 above $0.01$ (max $0.03$); the variables that predict raw returns do not predict the five-factor residuals.
conclusions: The five risk factors capture the variation in expected stock and bond returns
The constant-slope assumption appears reasonable for the test portfolios

nodes.name: January Seasonals Are Absorbed by Risk-Factor Seasonals
nodes.statement: Strong January effects in stock returns ($SMB$ and $HML$ have January premiums of $2.74\%$ and $2.29\%$ per month) and in low-grade bond returns are largely captured by January seasonals in the five risk factors; residual January effects survive only for the smallest-stock quintile.

nodes.name: Split-Sample Validation
nodes.statement: When stocks in each of the 25 size-$BE/ME$ portfolios are split into two disjoint halves, with one half forming dependent portfolios and the other half forming the explanatory $RM-RF$, $SMB$, $HML$, the slopes and three-factor intercepts are similar to the full-sample results, ruling out the concern that the explanatory power of $SMB$ and $HML$ is spuriously induced by the regression setup.

nodes.name: Three-Factor Model Explains E/P and D/P Portfolios
nodes.statement: For portfolios formed on $E/P$ and $D/P$, the one-factor Sharpe-Lintner model leaves systematic intercepts; the three-factor model produces intercepts close to $0$ for all five positive-$E/P$ and five positive-$D/P$ portfolios, with the cross-sectional spread in average returns absorbed by loadings on $HML$.

nodes.name: Low Correlation Between SMB and HML
nodes.statement: The 1963-1991 monthly correlation between $SMB$ and $HML$ is only $-0.08$, supporting the construction's goal of mimicking returns that isolate the size and book-to-market factors with minimal cross-contamination.

nodes.name: Average Risk Premiums Are Modest in Statistical Terms
nodes.statement: Average values: $RM-RF=0.43\%$ per month ($t=1.76$), $SMB=0.27\%$ ($t=1.73$), $HML=0.40\%$ ($t=2.91$), $TERM=0.06\%$ ($t=0.38$), $DEF=0.02\%$ ($t=0.21$); only $HML$ is statistically large.

nodes.name: Three-Factor Regression Failure for Smallest Growth Portfolio
nodes.statement: The GRS rejection of the three-factor model is concentrated in the smallest-$ME$ lowest-$BE/ME$ portfolio (intercept $-0.34\%$ per month, $t=-3.16$) and the largest-$ME$ lowest-$BE/ME$ portfolio (intercept $0.21\%$, $t=3.27$); reflects the absence of a size effect among growth stocks.

nodes.name: Economic Drivers of Size and BE/ME Risk Factors
nodes.statement: How are the size and book-to-market factors in returns driven by the stochastic behavior of earnings? Can specific fundamentals be identified as state variables that produce common variation in returns associated with $ME$ and $BE/ME$ that is not absorbed by the market return and carries a different premium than general market risk?

nodes.name: Application: Portfolio Performance Evaluation
nodes.statement: The intercept in a time-series regression of a managed portfolio's excess return on the five explanatory returns ($RM-RF$, $SMB$, $HML$, $TERM$, $DEF$) is the abnormal return needed to judge whether a manager beats passive combinations of the mimicking portfolios.

nodes.name: Application: Acquiring-Firm Abnormal Returns
nodes.statement: Agrawal, Jaffe, and Mandelker (1991) find persistent negative post-merger abnormal returns using a Sharpe-Lintner residual; the authors conjecture this is a book-to-market effect, since acquiring firms tend to be successful firms (low $BE/ME$) with low loadings on $HML$.
